title: trataka
hook: a child stares at a light bulb, squeezes her eyes shut, and finds a glowing shape still floating there

segments.voice: Yesterday, trataka and the Gita's lamp in a windless place: the flame still burns, only the flicker goes. When your attention leaned sideways, did you catch it and come back? Day one thousand twenty-eight.

A child lies on her bed staring straight up at the light bulb, because someone told her not to. Then she squeezes her eyes shut. And there it is: a glowing shape, floating in the dark behind her eyelids, green, then purple, drifting a little when she moves her eyes. She opens them, stares again, shuts them again, delighted. It's a game. In trataka, the same thing happens, and it isn't treated as a side effect. Some teachers make it the second half. Today, the turn from the flame on the table to the flame behind the eyes.
screen: `STARE AT THE LIGHT. SHUT THE EYES.` → `A GLOWING SHAPE STAYS.` → `NOT A SIDE EFFECT. THE SECOND HALF.`

segments.voice: Some teachers of trataka describe it in two parts. Outer trataka is the gaze on the flame or the mark, eyes open. Inner trataka begins when the eyes close. The image left behind is held in attention, gently, for as long as it lasts. When it fades, some teachers say to keep looking into the place where it was, or to open the eyes and gaze again. Outer, then inner. The practice moves the same object from in front of the eyes to behind them. Why bother? The Katha Upanishad has a line that names the problem the second half answers. In paraphrase: the Self-existent one pierced the openings of the senses outward, so a person looks outward, and not at the Self within. But a certain wise one, wanting the deathless, turned the eyes around and saw the Self within. That phrase, eyes turned around, is the heart of it. The senses are made to face out. Sight especially. All day it runs ahead of us, to the next screen, the next face, the next sign. The verse doesn't blame the eyes for that. It says that's how they were made. And then it describes someone who, for once, turns them back. Trataka does this in a very literal, very small way. The outer gaze gathers attention onto one point. Then the eyelids close, and that same attention, already gathered, is pointed inward at an image that exists only on the inside. It's a training run. Not the Upanishad's whole vision, but a way of feeling, for a minute, what it might mean to turn the eyes around.
screen: `OUTER TRATAKA: EYES OPEN, ON THE FLAME.` · `INNER TRATAKA: THE IMAGE BEHIND THE LIDS.` · `THE SENSES WERE MADE TO FACE OUT.` · `THE WISE ONE TURNED THE EYES AROUND.` · then, large: `FROM THE FLAME OUT THERE TO THE FLAME IN HERE.`

segments.voice: Set a candle flame or a small, bright mark at eye level, never the sun. Gaze at it softly for a few breaths, blinking when you need to. Then close the eyes and look for the image it left behind. Hold attention on it without squinting or chasing it. Notice its color, where it drifts, how it fades. When it's gone, rest in the dark where it was for a breath or two. Then open the eyes and gaze again. Outer, then inner. The bell holds the time.
Trataka. A still gaze at one small point. Today, both halves: the flame in front of the eyes, and the image held behind them.

Your line: something of it stays inside. Today, after looking at something you love, a face, a tree, a cup of tea, close your eyes for one breath and see what of it stays inside. Day one thousand twenty-eight.

howItsDone: Some teachers of trataka pair the open-eyed gaze at a flame with a closed-eyed phase, in which the practitioner holds the after-image in attention until it fades, then gazes again.

match.prompt: outer and inner — tap the pairs.
pairs: eyes open, gaze on the flame
the image held behind the lids
pierced outward, made to face out

myth: in trataka, the glowing shape behind the lids is just a side effect to ignore
some teachers make it the second half: inner trataka holds that image in attention.
the Katha Upanishad says the senses were made to face outward
it says the Self-existent one pierced the openings outward, so a person looks out, not within.
in the Katha Upanishad, people look outward simply by their own choice
it says the Self-existent made the openings face outward; the wise one who turns the eyes around is the rare exception.

fork.setup: you've gazed at the flame, and now your eyes are closed. a glowing shape floats there. what do you do?
options: rub the eyes to clear it away.
hold it in attention until it fades.
fork.reveal: in inner trataka the after-image is the object: held gently until it fades, then the gaze begins again.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: avritta-chakshuh, with eyes turned around. The Katha Upanishad's phrase for the wise one who looked within.

trapdoor: what you thought: trataka is only staring at a candle.
what it means: it moves the object from in front of the eyes to behind them, outer and then inner.
what a scholar hears: Katha Upanishad 4.1 (2.1.1), parāñci khāni, and the dhīra who is āvṛtta-cakṣuḥ.

notes: Audit: third myth rewritten. 'The Upanishad doesn't scold the eyes' sat uneasily with Shankara's gloss of vyatṛṇat as 'injured' (hiṃsitavān); the myth now tests what the verse plainly says (the Self-existent made the openings face outward; kaścid dhīraḥ, a rare wise one, turns them around). 'Scold' softened to 'blame' in the teach. Keeper: confirm the reading of vyatṛṇat.
Day 3 of the trataka block (1026–1032). Angle: outer and inner trataka (bahir/antar), read through Katha 4.1, the eyes turned around.
The outer/inner division of trataka is modern teacher guidance (for example in the Bihar School), not from the Hatha Yoga Pradipika; it is attributed to 'teachers' only. Confirm.

Katha 4.1 paraphrased (parāñci khāni vyatṛṇat svayambhūs ... kaścid dhīraḥ pratyagātmānam aikṣad āvṛttacakṣur amṛtatvam icchan). Max Müller's SBE 15 rendering exists but was not quoted because the exact wording wasn't certain.
Check the Devanagari and transliteration of āvṛttacakṣuḥ in the 'original' game.
The bridge from Katha 4.1 to inner trataka is the script's own ('a training run'); the Upanishad does not mention trataka.
